questions.problem: The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ -8 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=5$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{5},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ -8 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -16 \\ -40 & -20\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}20 & -80 \\ -80 & -100\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}20-\lambda  & -80 \\ -80 & -100-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (20-\lambda )(-100-\lambda )-6\,400 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+80\lambda -8\,400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -60)(\lambda +140) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =60,\,-140\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-140.
$$

questions.problem: The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $0.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The  maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$  

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem: The minimum value of $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9,$ is $-18.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -6 \\ -6 & -9\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -6 \\ -6 & -9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 \\ -6 & -9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & -18 \\ -18 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-18,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-18.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-18:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-18)I & =[\begin{aligned}18 & -18 \\ -18 & -9\end{aligned}]+18[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}36 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-18)I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
